title: Frequency-domain solvers
text:
From a general perspective, the frequency-domain solvers are used to analyze the dynamic response of structures subjected to harmonic loads. In the frequency domain, Mdof systems are described at a given angular frequency \(\omega\) by the following equation: \[
\left(\mathbf{K} + j\omega\mathbf{C} - \omega^2\mathbf{M}\right) \mathbf{x}(\omega) = \mathbf{F}(\omega).
\]

title: Frequency-domain solvers
text:
1 Frequency response function
The Frequency response function (FRF) is computed by assuming a unit harmonic load at the \(i\)-th degree of freedom (DOF) and zero loads at all other DOFs, meaning that \(\mathbf{F}(\omega) = \mathbf{I}\).
Consequently, broadly speaking, the FRF is defined by: \[
\mathbf{H}(\omega) = \left(\mathbf{K} + j\omega\mathbf{C} - \omega^2\mathbf{M}\right)^{-1}.
\] This method is known as the direct method.
Alternatively, the FRF can be computed using the modal method, which is based on the eigenvalue decomposition of the system matrices. The modal method is more efficient for large systems, as it reduces the problem to a smaller number of modes. In this case and assuming a modal damping ratio, the FRF is computed as: \[
\mathbf{H}(\omega) = \mathbf{\Phi}\left(\mathbf{\Omega}^2 - \omega^2\mathbf{I} + 2j\omega\mathbf{\Xi}\right)^{-1}\mathbf{\Phi}^T,
\] where \(\mathbf{\Phi}\) is the mass-normalized mode shapes matrix and \(\mathbf{\Omega}^2 = \text{diag}(\omega_1^2, \dots, \omega_n^2)\) and \(\mathbf{\Xi} = \text{diag}(\xi_1\omega_1, \dots, \xi_n\omega_n)\).






Note



As explained in State-Space solvers - Section 2.1, the FRF can be computed for a given set of response dofs and a given set of excitation dofs by introducing the appropriate selection matrices \(\mathbf{S}_o\) and \(\mathbf{S}_e\). In this case, the FRF is given by: \[
\mathbf{H}_{oe}(\omega) = \mathbf{S}_o\mathbf{H}(\omega)\mathbf{S}_e.
\]

title: Frequency-domain solvers
text:
2 Response spectrum
Similarly to the FRF, the response spectrum is a complex function that describes the steady-state response of a system to a sinusoidal input. At a given angular frequency \(\omega\), it is expressed as : \[
\mathbf{x}(\omega) = \left(\mathbf{K} + j\omega\mathbf{C} - \omega^2\mathbf{M}\right)^{-1} \mathbf{F}(\omega).
\] or equivalently from the modes of the system: \[
\mathbf{x}(\omega) = \mathbf{\Phi}\left(\mathbf{\Omega}^2 - \omega^2\mathbf{I} + 2j\omega\mathbf{\Omega}\right)^{-1}\mathbf{L},
\] where \(\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{\Phi}^\mathsf{T}\mathbf{F}(\omega)\) is the modal participation factor matrix1.

title: Sdof solvers
text:
The package provides a set of solvers to compute the time response of a single-degree-of-freedom (sdof) system.


The free response of a sdof system is the response of the system when it is subjected to initial conditions only. This means that the displacement of the mass is solution of the following ordinary differential equation: \[
\begin{cases}
  \ddot x(t) + 2 \xi\omega_0\dot x(t) + \omega_0^2 x(t) = 0 \\
  x(0) = x_0 \\
  \dot x(0) = v_0
\end{cases}.
\]
Depending on the value of the damping ratio \(\xi\) and \(\omega_0 > 0\), the system can have 4 different types of free response:

an undamped motion when \(\xi = 0\). In this case, the free response is: \[
x(t) = x_0\cos\omega_0 t + \frac{v_0}{\omega_0}\sin\omega_0 t
\]
an underdamped motion when \(0 < \xi < 1\). In this case, the free response is: \[
x(t) = \left[x_0\cos\Omega_0 t + \frac{v_0 + \xi\Omega_0 x_0}{\Omega_0}\sin\Omega_0 t\right]e^{-\xi\omega_0 t}
\] where \(\Omega_0 = \omega_0\sqrt{1 - \xi^2}\).
a critically damped motion when \(\xi = 1\). In this case, the free response is: \[
x(t) = \left[x_0 + (v_0 + \omega_0 x_0)t\right]e^{-\omega_0 t}
\]
an overdamped motion when \(\xi > 1\). In this case, the free response is: \[
x(t) = \left[x_0\text{cosh}(\beta t) + \frac{v_0 + \xi\omega_0 x_0}{\beta}\text{sinh}\beta t\right]e^{-\xi\omega_0 t},
\] where \(\beta = \omega_0\sqrt{\xi^2 - 1}\).

Finally, if \(\omega = 0\), the mass is free from constraints and the free response is: \[
x(t) = x_0 + v_0 t.
\]

# Structural parameters
m = 1.
f0 = 1.

# Time vector
t = 0.:0.01:10.

# Initial conditions

# Undamped system
sdof_nd = Sdof(m, f0, 0.)
prob_nd = SdofFreeTimeProblem(sdof_nd, u0, t)
x_nd = solve(prob_nd).u

# Underdamped system
sdof_ud = Sdof(m, f0, 0.1)
prob_ud = SdofFreeTimeProblem(sdof_ud, u0, t)
x_ud = solve(prob_ud).u

# Critically damped system

prob_cd = SdofFreeTimeProblem(sdof_cd, u0, t)
x_cd = solve(prob_cd).u

# Overdamped system
sdof_od = Sdof(m, f0, 1.2)
prob_od = SdofFreeTimeProblem(sdof_od, u0, t)
x_od = solve(prob_od).u;










The forced response of a sdof system is the response of the system is the solution of the following ordinary differential equation: \[
\begin{cases}
  \ddot x(t) + 2 \xi\omega_0\dot x(t) + \omega_0^2 x(t) = \displaystyle\frac{\text{rhs}(t)}{m} \\
  x(0) = x_0 \\
  \dot x(0) = v_0
\end{cases},
\] where \(\text{rhs}(t)\) is the right-hand side of the equation and its expression depends on the type of excitation: \[
\text{rhs}(t) = \begin{cases}
f(t) & \text{for an external force excitation} \\
m\omega_0^2 x_b(t) + 2\xi\omega_0m\dot x_b(t) & \text{for a base excitation}
\end{cases}.
\]
Finally, the solution of the forced response is expressed as the sum of two terms, since: \[
x(t) = x_h(t) + x_p(t),
\] where \(x_h(t)\) is the homogeneous solution of the equation and \(x_p(t)\) is the particular solution of the equation.


When the excitation is harmonic, the resolution process is the following:

Compute the particular solution of the equation. The particular solution is a harmonic function of the same frequency as the excitation.
Express the general solution of the homogeneous equation.
Compute the remaining constants using the initial conditions. These constants depends on \(x_p(0)\) and \(\dot x_p(0)\).

For an arbitrary excitation, the solution is given by: \[
x(t) = x_\text{free}(t) + \int_0^t rhs(t - τ)h(τ)dτ,
\] where \(x_\text{free}(t)\) is the free response of the system and \(h(t)\) is the impulse response of the system.

The shock response spectrum (SRS) is a graph of the peak acceleration response of a sdof system subjected to a base acceleration with respect to the frequency. The SRS is computed by solving the following problem: \[

\] where \(z(t) = x(t) - x_b(t)\) is the relative displacement of the system with respect to the base.

Instantiate a Sdof type

Compute the time response of the relative displacement \(z(t)\) due to a base acceleration for \(z(0) = 0\) and \(\dot z(0) = 0\).
Compute the acceleration \(\ddot x(t)\) of the system: \[

\]
Extract the primary or secondary part of the acceleration (i.e. until or after the end of the excitation signal).
Compute either:

The peak acceleration of the system such that: \[
SRS(f) = \max\left(|\ddot x(t)|\right)
\]
The maximum positive acceleration of the system such that: \[
SRS(f) = \max\left(\max(\ddot x(t), 0)\right)
\]
The maximum negative acceleration of the system such that: \[
SRS(f) = \max\left(\max(-\ddot x(t), 0)\right)
\]

:Basic: the SRS is computed by following the steps mentioned above. It is not the most efficient algorithm but it is the most versatile.
:RecursiveInt: the SRS is computed using a recursive integration algorithm.
:RecursiveFilt: the SRS is computed using a recursive filtering algorithm.
:Smallwood: the SRS is computed using the Smallwood algorithm.

title: Sdof solvers
text:
The package provides a set of solvers to compute the time response of a single-degree-of-freedom (sdof) system.


The free response of a sdof system is the response of the system when it is subjected to initial conditions only. This means that the displacement of the mass is solution of the following ordinary differential equation: \[
\begin{cases}
  \ddot x(t) + 2 \xi\omega_0\dot x(t) + \omega_0^2 x(t) = 0 \\
  x(0) = x_0 \\
  \dot x(0) = v_0
\end{cases}.
\]
Depending on the value of the damping ratio \(\xi\) and \(\omega_0 > 0\), the system can have 4 different types of free response:

an undamped motion when \(\xi = 0\). In this case, the free response is: \[
x(t) = x_0\cos\omega_0 t + \frac{v_0}{\omega_0}\sin\omega_0 t
\]
an underdamped motion when \(0 < \xi < 1\). In this case, the free response is: \[
x(t) = \left[x_0\cos\Omega_0 t + \frac{v_0 + \xi\Omega_0 x_0}{\Omega_0}\sin\Omega_0 t\right]e^{-\xi\omega_0 t}
\] where \(\Omega_0 = \omega_0\sqrt{1 - \xi^2}\).
a critically damped motion when \(\xi = 1\). In this case, the free response is: \[
x(t) = \left[x_0 + (v_0 + \omega_0 x_0)t\right]e^{-\omega_0 t}
\]
an overdamped motion when \(\xi > 1\). In this case, the free response is: \[
x(t) = \left[x_0\text{cosh}(\beta t) + \frac{v_0 + \xi\omega_0 x_0}{\beta}\text{sinh}\beta t\right]e^{-\xi\omega_0 t},
\] where \(\beta = \omega_0\sqrt{\xi^2 - 1}\).

Finally, if \(\omega = 0\), the mass is free from constraints and the free response is: \[
x(t) = x_0 + v_0 t.
\]


Data type

SdofFreeTimeProblem



SdofFreeTimeProblem(sdof, u0, t)
Structure containing the data of a time problem for a sdof system
Fields

v0: Initial velocity [m/s]

# Structural parameters

# Time vector

# Overdamped system

x_od = solve(prob_od).u;










The forced response of a sdof system is the response of the system is the solution of the following ordinary differential equation: \[
\begin{cases}
  \ddot x(t) + 2 \xi\omega_0\dot x(t) + \omega_0^2 x(t) = \displaystyle\frac{\text{rhs}(t)}{m} \\
  x(0) = x_0 \\
  \dot x(0) = v_0
\end{cases},
\] where \(\text{rhs}(t)\) is the right-hand side of the equation and its expression depends on the type of excitation: \[
\text{rhs}(t) = \begin{cases}
f(t) & \text{for an external force excitation} \\
m\omega_0^2 x_b(t) + 2\xi\omega_0m\dot x_b(t) & \text{for a base excitation}
\end{cases}.
\]
Finally, the solution of the forced response is expressed as the sum of two terms, since: \[
x(t) = x_h(t) + x_p(t),
\] where \(x_h(t)\) is the homogeneous solution of the equation and \(x_p(t)\) is the particular solution of the equation.


When the excitation is harmonic, the resolution process is the following:

Compute the particular solution of the equation. The particular solution is a harmonic function of the same frequency as the excitation.
Express the general solution of the homogeneous equation.
Compute the remaining constants using the initial conditions. These constants depends on \(x_p(0)\) and \(\dot x_p(0)\).

title: Sdof solvers
text:
2 Frequency domain solvers
The package provides solvers for computing the Frequency Response Function (FRF) and the response spectrum of a sdof system.

2.1 Frequency Response Function
The Frequency Response Function (FRF) of a sdof system is the ratio of the steady-state response \(X(\omega)\) of the system to an external excitation \(F(\omega)\) or an external base motion \(X_b(\omega)\). The FRF is computed from the following equation: \[
H(\omega) = \begin{cases}
\displaystyle\frac{1}{m(\omega_0^2 - \omega^2 + 2j\xi\omega\omega_0)} & \text{for a force excitation} \\
\displaystyle\frac{\omega_0^2 + 2j\xi\omega\omega_0}{\omega_0^2 - \omega^2 + 2j\xi\omega\omega_0} & \text{for a base excitation}
\end{cases},
\] where \(j\) is the imaginary unit.

2.1.1 API
Data type

SdofFRFProblem



SdofFRFProblem(sdof, freq, type_exc, type_resp)
Structure containing the data for computing the FRF a sdof system
Fields

type_exc::Symbol: Type of excitation

:force: External force (default)

:base: Base motion



type_resp::Symbol: Type of response

:dis: Admittance (default)

:vel: Mobility

:acc: Accelerance

2.1.2 Example

# Structural parameters
m = 1.
f0 = 10.
ξ = 0.01

# Instantiation of the Sdof object
sdof = Sdof(m, f0, ξ)

# Definition of the frequency range
f = 1.:0.1:30.

# Instantiation of the problem - Force excitation
prob = SdofFRFProblem(sdof, f)

# Solve the problem
H = solve(prob).u









2.2 Response spectrum
The response spectrum of a sdof system is the frequency response of the system to an external force \(F(\omega)\) or a base motion \(X_b(\omega)\) with respect to the frequency. The response spectrum \(Y(\omega)\) is computed from the following equation: \[
Y(\omega) = \begin{cases}
\displaystyle\frac{F(\omega)}{m(\omega_0^2 - \omega^2 + 2j\xi\omega\omega_0)} & \text{for a force excitation} \\
\displaystyle\frac{(\omega_0^2 + 2j\xi\omega\omega_0) X_b(\omega)}{\omega_0^2 - \omega^2 + 2j\xi\omega\omega_0} & \text{for a base excitation}
\end{cases}.
\]

title: Excitation models
text:
To define an excitation, two steps must be followed:

Initialize an excitation type:
exc_type = MyExcitation(params...)
Compute the excitation signal corresponding to the given excitation type over a given duration t (See Section 2 for details):
F = excitation(exc_type, t)



The rectangular signal is defined by the following equation: \[
F(t) = \begin{cases}
F_0 & \text{if } t \in [t_\text{start}, t_\text{start} + T] \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases},
\] where \(F_0\) is the amplitude of the signal, \(t_\text{start}\) is the start time of the signal, and \(T\) is the duration of the signal.

Rectangle



Rectangle(F, tstart, duration)
Struct to define a rectangular excitation signal
Fields

F::Real: Amplitude of the force [N]

tstart::Real: Starting time of the excitation [s]

duration::Real: Duration of the excitation [s]









# Time parameters
Δt = 1e-3
t = 0.:Δt:10.

# Excitation parameters
F0 = 1.
tstart = 2.5
duration = 5.

# Initialize Rectangle type
rect = Rectangle(F0, tstart, duration)

# Compute the excitation
F_rect = excitation(rect, t)









The triangle signal is defined by the following equation: \[
F(t) = \begin{cases}
\frac{2F_0}{T}\left(t - t_\text{start}\right) & \text{if } t \in [t_\text{start}, t_m] \\
F_0 - \frac{2F_0}{T}(t - t_m) & \text{if } t \in [t_m, t_\text{start} + T] \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases},
\] where \(F_0\) is the amplitude of the signal, \(t_\text{start}\) is the start time of the signal, \(T\) is the duration of the signal and \(t_m = t_\text{start} + T/2\) is the time at which the signal reaches its maximum value.

Triangle



Triangle(F, tstart, duration)
Struct to define a triangular excitation signal
Fields

F::Real: Amplitude of the force [N]

tstart::Real: Starting time of the excitation [s]

duration::Real: Duration of the excitation [s]









# Time parameters
Δt = 1e-3
t = 0.:Δt:10.

# Excitation parameters
F0 = 1.
tstart = 2.5
duration = 5.

# Initialize Triangle type
tri = Triangle(F0, tstart, duration)

# Compute the excitation
F_tri = excitation(tri, t)









The hammer impact signal is supposed to have the shape of a Gamma distribution \[
F(t) = \begin{cases}
F_0\left(\frac{t_h}{p\theta}\right)^p \text{exp}\left(-\frac{t_h}{\theta} + p\right), & \text{if } t \geq t_\text{start} \\
0, & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases},
\] where \(F_0\) is the amplitude of the signal, \(t_h = t - t_\text{start}\) is the time since the impact, \(p\) is the shape parameter, and \(\theta\) is the scale parameter.

Hammer



Hammer(F, tstart, k, θ)
Struct to define a hammer impact excitation signal
Fields

F::Real: Amplitude of the force [N]

tstart::Real: Starting time of the excitation [s]

p::Real: Shape parameter

θ::Real: Intensity parameter [s]









# Time parameters
Δt = 1e-5
t = 0.:Δt:0.05

# Excitation parameters
F0 = 1.
tstart = 0.01
k = 9.7
θ = 6e-4

# Initialize Hammer type

The smooth rectangular signal (custom Tukey window) is defined by the following equation: \[
F(t) = \begin{cases}

F_0 & \text{if } t \in [t_\text{start} + t_\text{rise}, t_\text{start} + t_\text{rise} + T_\text{rect}] \\
\frac{F_0}{2}\left[1 - \cos\left(\frac{2\pi (t - t_\text{start} - t_\text{rise} - T_\text{rect})}{\alpha T}\right)\right] & \text{if } t \in [t_\text{start} + t_\text{rise} + T_\text{rect}, t_\text{start} + T] \\
\end{cases},
\] where \(F_0\) is the amplitude of the signal, \(t_\text{start}\) is the start time of the signal, \(T\) is the duration of the signal, \(t_\text{rise}\) is the duration to reach \(F_0\) and \(\alpha = \frac{2t_\text{rise}}{T}\) and \(T_\text{rect} = T - 2t_\text{rise}\) is the duration of the rectangular part of the signal.

The sine signal is defined by the following equation: \[
F(t) = \begin{cases}

0, & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases},
\] where \(F_0\) is the amplitude of the signal, \(\omega\) is the angular frequency of the signal, and \(\theta\) is the phase of the signal.






NoteZero-end signal





Sometimes it is necessary to have a signal that ends at zero. In this case, the duration of the signal must be adjusted to ensure that the signal ends at zero. To do so, one have to find the smallest integer \(n\) such that at \(t = t_\text{start} + T\): \[
\sin(\omega T + \theta) = 0 \Rightarrow \omega T + \theta = 2\pi n \Rightarrow n = \frac{\omega T + \theta}{2\pi}.
\]
Once \(n\) is found, the duration of the signal must be adjusted to: \[
T_\text{new} = \frac{2\pi n - \theta}{\omega}.
\]

The swept sine signal is defined by the following equation: \[
F(t) = \begin{cases}
F_0 \sin(\theta(t)) & \text{if } t \in [t_\text{start}, t_\text{start} + T] \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases},
\] where \(F_0\) is the amplitude of the signal, \(t_\text{start}\) is the start time of the signal, \(T\) is the duration of the signal and \(\theta(t)\) is the instantaneous phase.
The instantaneous phase is given by: \[
\theta(t) = \theta_0 + 2\pi\int_0^t f(\tau) d\tau,
\] where \(f(\tau)\) is the instantaneous frequency of the signal at time \(\tau\) and \(\theta_0\) is the initial phase (set to 0 here).
In this package, three possible types of swept sine signals are available:

Linear swept sine: \[
f(t) = f_\text{start} + \beta(t - t_\text{start}) \Rightarrow \theta(t) = 2\pi\left(f_\text{start}(t - t_\text{start}) + \frac{\beta (t - t_\text{start})^2}{2}\right),
\] where:

\(\beta = \frac{f_\text{end} - f_\text{start}}{T}\)
\(f_\text{start}\): Initial frequency of the signal at \(t_\text{start}\)
\(f_\text{end}\): Final frequency of the signal at \(t_\text{start} + T\)

Quadratic swept sine: \[
f(t) = f_\text{start} + \beta (t - t_\text{start})^2 \Rightarrow \theta(t) = 2\pi\left(f_\text{start}(t - t_\text{start}) + \frac{\beta (t - t_\text{start})^3}{3}\right),
\] where \(\beta = \frac{f_\text{end} - f_\text{start}}{T^2}\).
Logarithmic swept sine: \[
f(t) = f_\text{start}\beta^{t - t_\text{start}} \Rightarrow \theta(t) = \frac{2\pi f_\text{start}}{\log(\beta)}\left(\beta^{t - t_\text{start}} - 1\right),
\] where \(\beta = \left(\frac{f_\text{end}}{f_\text{start}}\right)^{1/T}\).







NoteZero-end signal





Similarly to the sine signal, the duration of the signal must be adjusted to ensure that the signal ends at zero. To do so, one have to find the smallest integer \(n\) such that at \(t = t_\text{start} + T\): \[
  \theta(t) = 2\pi n.
\]
In doing so, we have for:

Linear swept sine: \[
n = (f_\text{start} + f_\text{end})\frac{T}{2} \Rightarrow T_\text{new} = \frac{2n}{f_\text{start} + f_\text{end}}.
\]
Quadratic swept sine: \[
n = (2f_\text{start} + f_\text{end})\frac{T}{3} \Rightarrow T_\text{new} = \frac{3n}{2f_\text{start} + f_\text{end}}.
\]
Logarithmic swept sine: \[
n = \frac{f_\text{end} - f_\text{start}}{\log(f_\text{end}/f_\text{start})}T \Rightarrow T_\text{new} = \frac{n\log(f_\text{end}/f_\text{start})}{f_\text{end} - f_\text{start}}.
\]

The Gaussian pulse signal is defined by the following equation: \[
F(t) = \begin{cases}
F_0 \exp\left(-\frac{t_p^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) \cos(2\pi f_c t_p), & \text{if } t \geq t_\text{start} \\
0, & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases},
\] where \(F_0\) is the amplitude of the signal, \(t_\text{start}\) is the start time of the signal, \(\sigma\) is the standard deviation of the signal, and \(f_c\) is the carrier frequency. Here \(t_p = t - t_\text{start} - T/2\) so that the Gaussian pulse reaches its maximum value at \(t = t_\text{start} + T/2\).






NoteVariance calibration





The design of the Gaussian pulse assumes that it tends to zero when \(t = t_\text{start} + T\). This requirement implies that the standard deviation \(\sigma\) must be chosen such that the Gaussian pulse is zero at \(t = t_\text{start} + T\). This condition can only be satisfied within some precision. More precisely, the idea is to find the quantile \(n\) such that \(T = n\sigma\). Consequently, if we assume that \(F(t_\text{start} + T) = 10^{-p}\) (with \(p\) a given precision), we have: \[
n = 2\sqrt{2(p\log 10 + \log F_0)} \Rightarrow \sigma = \frac{T}{n}.
\]

The precision parameter calibrates the standard deviation of the pulse, so that the duration = n x σ, within some precision. If n = 1.96 then the confidence interval of the Gaussian distribution is 95%. To do so, we compute n so that at t = duration = n x σ , the amplitude of F x exp(-0.5*(t - duration/2)^2/sigma^2) = 10^(-precision)

Colored noise is a random signal that has a power spectral density that is not (necessarily) flat over a given frequency range. In practice, colored noise is also refered to as “power-law noise” since its power spectral density is proportional to \(f^{-\alpha}\) (\(f\): frequency) and its spectrum is proportional to \(f^{-\alpha/2}\).
In this package, five types of colored noise are available:

White noise: \(\alpha = 0\)
Pink noise: \(\alpha = 1\)
Blue noise: \(\alpha = -1\)
Brown noise: \(\alpha = 2\)
Purple noise: \(\alpha = -2\)

The general procedure to generate a colored noise signal is as follows:

Generate a white noise signal and compute its FFT
Multiply the FFT by \(f^{-\alpha/2}\) to obtain the colored noise
Compute the inverse FFT to obtain the colored noise signal

Additional steps can be added such as:

Normalization: Ensure that the colored noise has the desired variance and preserves the energy of the white noise
Filtering: Obtain a band-limited colored noise

:white (default)

:pink

:blue

:brown

:purple

exc_blue = ColoredNoise(F0, tstart, duration, σ, color = :blue)

# Compute the spectrum of the colored noise

S_white = rfft(excitation(exc_white, t))
S_pink = rfft(excitation(exc_pink, t))
S_blue = rfft(excitation(exc_blue, t))
S_brown = rfft(excitation(exc_brown, t))
S_purple = rfft(excitation(exc_purple, t))

In doing so, we have for:

Linear swept sine: \[
n = (f_\text{start} + f_\text{end})\frac{T}{2} \Rightarrow T_\text{new} = \frac{2n}{f_\text{start} + f_\text{end}}.
\]
Quadratic swept sine: \[
n = (2f_\text{start} + f_\text{end})\frac{T}{3} \Rightarrow T_\text{new} = \frac{3n}{2f_\text{start} + f_\text{end}}.
\]
Logarithmic swept sine: \[
n = \frac{f_\text{end} - f_\text{start}}{\log(f_\text{end}/f_\text{start})}T \Rightarrow T_\text{new} = \frac{n\log(f_\text{end}/f_\text{start})}{f_\text{end} - f_\text{start}}.
\]





SweptSine



SweptSine(F, tstart, duration, fstart, fend, type)

:lin - linear (default)

Δt = 1e-3

The Gaussian pulse signal is defined by the following equation: \[
F(t) = \begin{cases}
F_0 \exp\left(-\frac{t_p^2}{2\sigma^2}\right) \cos(2\pi f_c t_p), & \text{if } t \geq t_\text{start} \\
0, & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases},
\] where \(F_0\) is the amplitude of the signal, \(t_\text{start}\) is the start time of the signal, \(\sigma\) is the standard deviation of the signal, and \(f_c\) is the carrier frequency. Here \(t_p = t - t_\text{start} - T/2\) so that the Gaussian pulse reaches its maximum value at \(t = t_\text{start} + T/2\).






NoteVariance calibration





The design of the Gaussian pulse assumes that it tends to zero when \(t = t_\text{start} + T\). This requirement implies that the standard deviation \(\sigma\) must be chosen such that the Gaussian pulse is zero at \(t = t_\text{start} + T\). This condition can only be satisfied within some precision. More precisely, the idea is to find the quantile \(n\) such that \(T = n\sigma\). Consequently, if we assume that \(F(t_\text{start} + T) = 10^{-p}\) (with \(p\) a given precision), we have: \[
n = 2\sqrt{2(p\log 10 + \log F_0)} \Rightarrow \sigma = \frac{T}{n}.
\]




GaussianPulse



GaussianPulse(F, tstart, duration, fc)
Struct to define a Gaussian pulse excitation signal
Fields

F::Real: Amplitude of the force [N]

tstart::Real: Starting time of the excitation [s]

duration::Real: Duration of the excitation [s]

fc::Real: Center frequency of the pulse [Hz]

precision::Real: Precision of the pulse (default = 4.)


Note
The precision parameter calibrates the standard deviation of the pulse, so that the duration = n x σ, within some precision. If n = 1.96 then the confidence interval of the Gaussian distribution is 95%. To do so, we compute n so that at t = duration = n x σ , the amplitude of F x exp(-0.5*(t - duration/2)^2/sigma^2) = 10^(-precision)







# Time parameters
Δt = 1e-3
t = 0.:Δt:10.

# Excitation parameters
F0 = 1.
tstart = 2.5
duration = 5.
fc = 2.

# Initialize GaussianPulse type
gpulse = GaussianPulse(F0, tstart, duration, fc)

# Compute the excitation
F_gpulse = excitation(gpulse, t)









Colored noise is a random signal that has a power spectral density that is not (necessarily) flat over a given frequency range. In practice, colored noise is also refered to as “power-law noise” since its power spectral density is proportional to \(f^{-\alpha}\) (\(f\): frequency) and its spectrum is proportional to \(f^{-\alpha/2}\).
In this package, five types of colored noise are available:

White noise: \(\alpha = 0\)
Pink noise: \(\alpha = 1\)
Blue noise: \(\alpha = -1\)
Brown noise: \(\alpha = 2\)
Purple noise: \(\alpha = -2\)

The general procedure to generate a colored noise signal is as follows:

Generate a white noise signal and compute its FFT
Multiply the FFT by \(f^{-\alpha/2}\) to obtain the colored noise
Compute the inverse FFT to obtain the colored noise signal

Additional steps can be added such as:

Normalization: Ensure that the colored noise has the desired variance and preserves the energy of the white noise
Filtering: Obtain a band-limited colored noise


ColoredNoise



ColoredNoise(F, color)
Struct to define a colored noise excitation signal
Fields

F::Real: Mean amplitude of the force [N]

tstart::Real: Starting time of the excitation [s]

duration::Real: Duration of the excitation [s]

σ::Real: Target standard deviation of the colored noise

color::Symbol: Color of the noise

:white (default)

:pink

:blue

:brown

:purple



frange::AbstractVector: Frequencies used to defined the bandpass filter applied to the colored noise









using FFTW

# Time parameters
Δt = 1e-4
t = 0.:Δt:10.
nt = length(t)
fs = 1/Δt

# Excitation parameters
F0 = 1.
tstart = 0.
duration = 10.
σ = 1.

# Initialize ColoredNoise type
exc_white = ColoredNoise(F0, tstart, duration, σ, color = :white)
exc_pink = ColoredNoise(F0, tstart, duration, σ, color = :pink)
exc_blue = ColoredNoise(F0, tstart, duration, σ, color = :blue)
exc_brown = ColoredNoise(F0, tstart, duration, σ, color = :brown)
exc_purple = ColoredNoise(F0, tstart, duration, σ, color = :purple)

# Compute the spectrum of the colored noise
freq = rfftfreq(nt, fs)
S_white = rfft(excitation(exc_white, t))
S_pink = rfft(excitation(exc_pink, t))
S_blue = rfft(excitation(exc_blue, t))
S_brown = rfft(excitation(exc_brown, t))
S_purple = rfft(excitation(exc_purple, t))

title: Noise models
text: In real-world applications, the noise is always present in the measured data. The noise can be due to various reasons such as the sensor noise, the environmental noise, the quantization noise, etc. The noise can be modeled as a random process. The package implements various type of noise in order to cover a wide range of practical situations.

title: Noise models
text:
1 Additive Gaussian White noise
When a signal, real or complex, \(x\) is corrupted by an additive Gaussian white noise \(n\), the measured signal \(y\) can be written as: \[
    y = x + n
\] where \(n \sim \mathcal{N}(n| 0, \sigma^2)\)

title: Extensions
text:
2 Mesh manipulation
To access the mesh manipulation functions, you need to activate the SVMeshExt.jl extension by running the following command:
using Meshes
This extension provides functions for mesh manipulation, such as building a mesh from nodes and elements, detrending a plane or a mesh, visualizing a mesh, deforming a grid, and renumbering the element connectivity.

2.1 Building a mesh
The build_mesh function allows you to build a mesh from nodes and elements. The function takes as input the nodes and the elements of the mesh and returns a SimpleMesh object from Meshes.jl.

build_mesh

Generate mesh points and connectivity from node coordinates and element connectivity.

Outputs

Notes

This function is restricted to 2D meshes where elements are either triangles or quadrilaterals.










2.2 Detrending a plane or a mesh
The detrend_plane and detrend_mesh functions allow you to detrend a plane or a mesh, respectively. The detrending process implemented in detrend_plane consists in fitting a plane to the data and substracting the fitted plane from the data. The detrend_mesh function first removes the mean from the mesh and then applies the detrend_plane function to the each plane.

2.3 Deforming a grid
The deformed_grid function allows you to deform a grid of points by applying a set of values to its nodes. This is useful, for instance, for visualizing the deformation or mode shapes of a structure.

2.4 Renumbering the element connectivity
The renumber_element_connectivity function allows you to renumber the element connectivity of a mesh. This is useful when the element connectivity is not consistent with the node numbering. Indeed, Meshes.jl implicitly states that the nodes in a mesh are numbered from 1 to the number of nodes, and that the element connectivity is defined accordingly. If this is not the case, the renumber_element_connectivity function can be used to renumber the element connectivity to be consistent with the node numbering.

renumber_element_connectivity(elts, nodes_ID)
Renumber elements connectivity based on a given list of node IDs.
Inputs

nodes_ID::Vector{Int}: The list of node IDs.


Outputs

Notes

This function assumes that each node ID in nodes_ID corresponds to a unique node in the original mesh and that the element connectivity in elts references these node IDs.

The renumbering is necessary if the elements ID are not contiguous or if they do not start from 1, which can cause issues when using Meshes.jl for visualization or further processing.

Notes

When values is a vector of values and frequency is specified, the animation simulates a harmonic motion of the mesh based on the provided values and frequency. This is useful for visualizing mode shapes or operational deflection shapes in structural vibration analysis.

When values is a matrix and x is provided, the animation shows the evolution of the mesh deformation as a function of the parameter x, which can represent time, frequency, or any other relevant parameter. The title of the animation updates dynamically every 10 frames to reflect the current value of x.










3.3 Example
In this example, we will visualize the second mode shape of a simply supported plate.

3.3.1 Data generation

using LazyGrids

# Dimensions
Lp = 0.6
bp = 0.4
hp = 1e-3

# Material parameters
E = 2.1e11
ρ = 7800.
ν = 0.33

plate = Plate(Lp, bp, hp, E, ρ, ν)



3.3.2 Mesh creation

# Helper function to create a quadrilateral mesh
function create_quad_mesh(xp::Vector, yp::Vector, nx::Int, ny::Int)
    # Number of quadrangles
    n_quads = (nx - 1) * (ny - 1)
    quads = Vector{Vector{Int}}(undef, n_quads)

    quad_idx = 1
    for j in 1:(ny-1)
        for i in 1:(nx-1)
            # Indices of the nodes of the quadrangle in counter-clockwise order
            n1 = (j-1) * nx + i
            n2 = (j-1) * nx + i + 1
            n3 = j * nx + i + 1
            n4 = j * nx + i

            quads[quad_idx] = [n1, n2, n3, n4]
            quad_idx += 1
        end
    end

    return quads
end

# Create the mesh
nx = 10
ny = 10
x, y = ndgrid(range(0., Lp, nx), range(0., bp, ny))
xp = x[:]
yp = y[:]
zp = zeros(length(xp))

nodes = [xp yp zp]
elts = create_quad_mesh(xp, yp, nx, ny)
mesh = build_mesh(nodes, elts)

fig_mesh = viz_mesh(mesh, zlim = (-0.15, 0.15), title = "Mesh of the plate")






3.3.3 Visualization of the mode shape

# Compute the second mode shape
ms = sin.(2π*xp/Lp) .* sin.(π*yp/bp)

# Compute deformed grid
ms_deformed = zeros(3size(nodes, 1))
ms_deformed[3:3:end] .= ms

dpoints = deformed_grid(nodes, ms_deformed, 0.15)

fig_deformed = viz_mesh(SimpleMesh(dpoints, mesh.topology.connec), color = ms, zlim = (-0.2, 0.2), title = "Deformed mesh of the plate")






3.3.4 Animating the mode shape
animate_mesh(nodes, elts, ms_deformed, color = ms, scale_factor = 0.1, zlim = (-0.2, 0.2), title = "Second mode shape of a simply supported rectangular plate", framerate = 24, filename = "animated_plate.mp4")
Video

StructuralVibration.jl provides the Paraview Fast Colormap as a color gradient that can be used for visualizations. The colormap is implemented in the fast_cmap function.

title: Noise estimation and denoising
text:
NoteIn this tutorial




You will learn how to estimate the noise level of a measured signal without knowing the noise-free signal, and how to choose a denoising method.
Prerequisites: the Getting started page.
Duration: about 15 minutes.
Many post-processing operations are very sensitive to noise: numerical differentiation, inverse problems (force identification, model updating, …), or Kalman filtering, whose tuning requires the noise covariance. Knowing the noise level of a signal, and being able to reduce it, is therefore an essential step. As usual, we work with synthetic data so that every result can be compared with the truth.

title: Noise estimation and denoising
text:
1 Step 1 – A noisy measurement
A simply supported beam is hit by an impact hammer at \(x\) = 0.35 m, and its displacement is recorded at four points during 0.5 s.

using LinearAlgebra, Statistics

# Structure and sensors
L, b, h = 1., 0.03, 0.01
beam = Beam(L, b*h, b*h^3/12, 2.1e11, 7850.)
ξ = 0.01
x_sensors = [0.2, 0.35, 0.5, 0.7]

fs = 4096
ωn, kn = modefreq(beam, fs/2)
Φ_s = modeshape(beam, kn, x_sensors)
Φ_e = modeshape(beam, kn, [0.35])
nmodes = length(ωn)

# Impact response
t = 0.:1/fs:0.5
F = reshape(excitation(Hammer(100., 0., 9.7, 1e-4), t), 1, :)
prob = ForcedModalTimeProblem(ωn, Φ_s, ξ, Φ_e'*F, (zeros(nmodes), zeros(nmodes)), t)
sol = solve(prob)
x_true, v_true = sol.u, sol.du # Noise-free displacement and velocity

# Measurement: 20 dB SNR on each channel
SNR_true = 20.
y = agwn(x_true, SNR_true)


fig = Figure()
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "Time (s)", ylabel = "Displacement (m)", title = "Sensor at x = 0.2 m")
lines!(ax, t, y[1, :], color = (:gray, 0.6), label = "Measured")
lines!(ax, t, x_true[1, :], label = "Noise-free")
xlims!(ax, 0., 0.5)
axislegend(ax, position = :rt)
fig

title: Noise estimation and denoising
section: 2 Step 2 – Why noise matters: numerical differentiation
text:
2 Step 2 – Why noise matters: numerical differentiation
Suppose we need the velocity, but only the displacement was measured. Differentiating the measured signal is the obvious solution.

rel_error(a, ref) = [norm(a[i, :] - ref[i, :])/norm(ref[i, :]) for i in axes(ref, 1)]

v_noisy = gradient(y, t) # Differentiation along time (dims = 1: one signal per row)


println("Displacement error (measured):       ", round.(100rel_error(y, x_true), digits = 1), " %")
println("Velocity error (differentiated):     ", round.(100rel_error(v_noisy, v_true), digits = 1), " %")

Displacement error (measured):       [10.0, 10.1, 10.2, 9.8] %
Velocity error (differentiated):     [260.3, 294.8, 334.3, 277.3] %


A 10 % error on the displacement becomes an error of several hundred percent on the velocity. Differentiation amplifies the high-frequency content of the signal, where the noise dominates. This is typical of an ill-posed operation, and the reason why noise must be handled before such operations.

title: Noise estimation and denoising
text:
3 Step 3 – Estimating the noise level
In practice, the noise-free signal is unknown, and so is the noise level. varest estimates the noise variance of each channel from the measured signal only. Several methods are available:

BayesianEst() (default): a Bayesian version of the regularized smoothing.
DerricoEst(): a fast statistical estimator, based on finite differences of the signal;
GCVEst() and LCurveEst(): estimators based on the regularized smoothing of the signal, whose regularization parameter is selected by Generalized Cross-Validation or by the L-curve criterion;


methods = [("Bayesian", BayesianEst()), ("D'Errico", DerricoEst()), ("GCV", GCVEst()), ("L-curve", LCurveEst())]
SNR_est = [(name, estimated_SNR(y, varest(y, m))) for (name, m) in methods]


nch = length(SNR_est[1][2])
data = vcat(hcat("True", fill(SNR_true, 1, nch)),
            [hcat(name, round.(snr, digits = 1)') for (name, snr) in SNR_est]...)

pretty_table(
    HTML,
    data,
    column_labels = ["Method"; ["Channel $i (dB)" for i in 1:nch]],
    alignment = :c
)

Bayesian, D’Errico and GCV estimators recover the SNR within about 1 dB. The L-curve estimator is less reliable here: it tends to over-smooth the signal, and thus to overestimate the noise level.

title: Noise estimation and denoising
text:
4 Step 4 – Denoising
The same ideas lead to denoising methods. Regularization-based methods solve \[
\widehat{\mathbf{x}} = \underset{\mathbf{x}}{\text{argmin}} \Vert \mathbf{y} - \mathbf{x} \Vert_2^2 + \lambda \Vert \mathbf{D} \mathbf{x} \Vert_2^2,
\] where \(\mathbf{D}\) is a second-order difference operator that penalizes non-smooth signals and \(\lambda\) is selected automatically. Kalman-based methods model the signal as the output of a random-walk state-space model, the noise variance being estimated with varest. The rts = true option adds a backward pass (Rauch-Tung-Striebel smoother), which uses the whole signal to estimate each sample.

denoisers = [("GCV", GCVDenoising()), ("L-curve", LCurveDenoising()), ("Bayesian", BayesDenoising()),
             ("Kalman filter", KalmanDenoising()), ("Kalman smoother", KalmanDenoising(rts = true))]
x_dn = Dict(name => denoising(y, alg) for (name, alg) in denoisers)


nch = size(x_true, 1)
data = vcat(hcat("Measured signal", round.(100rel_error(y, x_true), digits = 1)'),
            [hcat(name, round.(100rel_error(x_dn[name], x_true), digits = 1)') for (name, _) in denoisers]...)

pretty_table(
    HTML,
    data,
    column_labels = ["Signal"; ["Channel $i error (%)" for i in 1:nch]],
    alignment = :c
)

fig = Figure()
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "Time (s)", ylabel = "Displacement (m)", title = "Sensor at x = 0.2 m – zoom")
lines!(ax, t, y[1, :], color = (:gray, 0.4), label = "Measured")
lines!(ax, t, x_true[1, :], color = :black, label = "Noise-free")
lines!(ax, t, x_dn["GCV"][1, :], linestyle = :dash, label = "GCV")
lines!(ax, t, x_dn["Kalman smoother"][1, :], linestyle = :dot, label = "Kalman smoother")
xlims!(ax, 0., 0.1)

fig




GCV and Bayesian regularization divide the error by about three, the Kalman smoother by about two. The Kalman filter alone, which only uses past samples, is less accurate, but it can be applied in real time. As for noise estimation, the L-curve criterion over-smooths some channels.

title: Noise estimation and denoising
text:
5 Step 5 – Back to differentiation

v_dn = gradient(x_dn["GCV"], t)
println("Velocity error from measured signal:  ", round.(100rel_error(v_noisy, v_true), digits = 1), " %")
println("Velocity error from denoised signal:  ", round.(100rel_error(v_dn, v_true), digits = 1), " %")

Velocity error from measured signal:  [260.3, 294.8, 334.3, 277.3] %
Velocity error from denoised signal:  [21.0, 24.1, 13.1, 19.6] %



fig = Figure()
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "Time (s)", ylabel = "Velocity (m/s)", title = "Sensor at x = 0.2 m")
lines!(ax, t, v_noisy[1, :], color = (:gray, 0.4), label = "From measured signal")
lines!(ax, t, v_true[1, :], color = :black, label = "Exact")
lines!(ax, t, v_dn[1, :], linestyle = :dash, label = "From denoised signal")
xlims!(ax, 0., 0.1)
axislegend(ax, position = :rt)
fig




Denoising before differentiating reduces the velocity error by more than an order of magnitude.

title: Noise estimation and denoising
text:
6 Summary







Need
Recommended tool




Quick estimate of the noise level
varest(y) (D’Errico)


More accurate estimate
varest(y, GCVEst()) or varest(y, BayesianEst())


Offline denoising
denoising(y, GCVDenoising()) or denoising(y, BayesDenoising())


Real-time or streaming denoising
denoising(y, KalmanDenoising())


Offline denoising of long signals
denoising(y, KalmanDenoising(rts = true))



The SNR of a signal is given by estimated_SNR(y, varest(y)), which is a useful sanity check of any measurement.
Reference pages: Noise estimation and denoising, Noise models.

title: Getting started
text: This page takes you from installation to your first results in about ten minutes. No prior knowledge of the package is assumed and basic notions of vibration (mass, stiffness, damping, resonance) are enough.

title: Getting started
text:
1 Installation
julia> ]
pkg> add StructuralVibration, CairoMakie
CairoMakie.jl is optional but it activates the plotting functions of the package (bode_plot, stabilization_plot, …). Any other Makie backend (GLMakie.jl, WGLMakie.jl) works as well.
using StructuralVibration, CairoMakie

title: Getting started
text:
2 Step 1 – Define a model
We start with the simplest vibrating system: a mass \(m\) attached to a spring and a viscous damper. It is fully described by its mass, its natural frequency \(f_0\) and its damping ratio \(\xi\).

m  = 1.     # Mass (kg)
f0 = 10.    # Natural frequency (Hz)
ξ  = 0.02   # Damping ratio (2 %)

sdof = Sdof(m, f0, ξ)

title: Getting started
text:
3 Step 2 – Free response
Let us pull the mass away from its equilibrium position and release it. The problem gathers the model, the initial conditions [x₀, v₀] and the time vector.

t  = 0.:1e-3:2.
u0 = [1e-3, 0.]    # Initial displacement (m) and velocity (m/s)

prob_free = SdofFreeTimeProblem(sdof, u0, t)
x_free = solve(prob_free).u


sv_plot(t, x_free, xlabel = "Time (s)", ylabel = "Displacement (m)")




The system oscillates at (almost) \(f_0\) = 10 Hz and the amplitude decays because of damping. Try ξ = 0. or ξ = 1. to see an undamped and a critically damped system.

title: Getting started
text:
4 Step 3 – Forced response
Now, we excite the mass with a harmonic force \(F(t) = F_0 \sin(2\pi f t)\). Only the problem changes: the model and the call to solve stay the same.

F0 = 10.   # Force amplitude (N)
f  = 9.5   # Excitation frequency (Hz), close to resonance

prob_harmo = SdofHarmonicTimeProblem(sdof, u0, t, F0, f, :force)
x_harmo = solve(prob_harmo).u


sv_plot(t, x_harmo, xlabel = "Time (s)", ylabel = "Displacement (m)")




The response combines a decaying transient (free response) and a steady-state oscillation at the excitation frequency. Arbitrary excitations (impacts, sweeps, random noise) are handled by SdofForcedTimeProblem together with the signals described in Excitation models.

title: Getting started
text:
5 Step 4 – Frequency Response Function
Rather than computing one response per excitation frequency, we usually characterize a structure by its Frequency Response Function (FRF) \(H(f)\), the ratio between the displacement and the force at each frequency.

freq = 1.:0.05:30.

prob_frf = SdofFRFProblem(sdof, freq)
H = solve(prob_frf).u


bode_plot(freq, H, isdeg = true)




The resonance peak is located at \(f_0\) and its sharpness is governed by \(\xi\). The phase shifts by 180° when crossing the resonance.

title: Getting started
text:
6 Step 5 – Same pattern, real structure
The four steps remain the same for continuous structures. Here, we compute the FRFs of a simply supported steel beam from its modes, add measurement noise, and identify its natural frequencies back, as an experimentalist would.

# 1. Model - Simply supported beam
L, b, h = 1., 0.03, 0.01
beam = Beam(L, b*h, b*h^3/12, 2.1e11, 7850.)

fmax = 500.
ωn, kn = modefreq(beam, 2fmax)       # Natural frequencies and wavenumbers
xm, xe = [0.2, 0.7], [0.35]          # Measurement and excitation points
ms_m, ms_e = modeshape(beam, kn, xm), modeshape(beam, kn, xe)

# 2. Problem + 3. Solve - Accelerances by modal superposition
freq = 1.:0.25:fmax
ξn = 0.01
prob = ModalFRFProblem(ωn, ξ, freq, ms_m, ms_e)
H = solve(prob, type = :acc, progress = false).u

# 4. Post-process - Noisy "measurement" (SNR = 40 dB) + modal identification
H_meas = agwn(H, 40.)
poles = poles_extraction(EMAProblem(H_meas, freq, type_frf = :acc), 20, LSCF())
fn_id, ξn_id = poles2modal(poles)

We computed accelerances (acceleration/force) because this is what an accelerometer and an impact hammer actually measure.

fig = Figure()
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "Frequency (Hz)", ylabel = "Accelerance (dB, ref: 1 m/s²/N)")
lines!(ax, freq, to_dB.(H_meas[1, 1, :]), label = "Noisy FRF")
lines!(ax, freq, to_dB.(H[1, 1, :]), label = "Exact FRF")
vlines!(ax, fn_id, color = :green, linestyle = :dash, label = "Identified modes")
xlims!(ax, freq[1], freq[end])
axislegend(ax, position = :rb)
fig





fn_exact = ωn[ωn .≤ 2π*fmax]/2π
println("Exact frequencies (Hz):      ", round.(fn_exact, digits = 2))
println("Identified frequencies (Hz): ", round.(fn_id, digits = 2))
println("Identified damping (%):      ", round.(100ξn_id, digits = 2))

Exact frequencies (Hz):      [23.45, 93.81, 211.08, 375.25]
Identified frequencies (Hz): [23.45, 93.82, 211.08, 375.27]
Identified damping (%):      [2.0, 1.99, 2.02, 2.0]


In twenty lines, we went from a structural model to synthetic measurements and back to modal parameters with a known ground truth. This round trip is what the package is designed for.

title: Visualizing and animating deflection shapes
text:
NoteIn this tutorial




You will learn how to build a measurement mesh, display mode shapes and operational deflection shapes (ODS) on it, and turn them into animations.
Prerequisites: the Getting started page. Basic knowledge of Makie is helpful.
Duration: about 15 minutes.
The visualization tools of StructuralVibration.jl are provided by package extensions, which are activated by loading Makie (any backend) and Meshes.jl:

title: Visualizing and animating deflection shapes
text:
1 Step 1 – The structure
We consider a simply supported steel plate of 600 × 400 × 1 mm. The analytical Plate model gives its natural frequencies and the corresponding wavenumbers.

plate = Plate(0.6, 0.4, 1e-3, 2.1e11, 7800., 0.33)   # Lx, Ly, thickness, E, ρ, ν
ωn, kn = modefreq(plate, 300.)[1:2]

# Mode indices (m, n): number of half-waves along x and y
mn = round.(Int, [kn[1, :]*0.6/π kn[2, :]*0.4/π])
for i in 1:6
    println("Mode $i: (m, n) = ($(mn[i, 1]), $(mn[i, 2])), f = ", round(ωn[i]/2π, digits = 1), " Hz")
end

Mode 1: (m, n) = (1, 1), f = 22.5 Hz
Mode 2: (m, n) = (2, 1), f = 43.3 Hz
Mode 3: (m, n) = (1, 2), f = 69.2 Hz
Mode 4: (m, n) = (3, 1), f = 77.9 Hz
Mode 5: (m, n) = (2, 2), f = 90.0 Hz
Mode 6: (m, n) = (3, 2), f = 124.6 Hz

title: Visualizing and animating deflection shapes
text:
2 Step 2 – Building a measurement mesh
A mesh is defined by a matrix of node coordinates (one row per node, columns \(x\), \(y\), \(z\)) and a list of elements, each element being the vector of its node indices. Here, we use a regular grid of 13 × 9 points and quadrangular elements.

using LazyGrids

nx, ny = 13, 9
X, Y = ndgrid(range(0., 0.6, nx), range(0., 0.4, ny))
xp, yp = X[:], Y[:]
nodes = [xp yp zeros(length(xp))]

# Quadrangles, with nodes listed counter-clockwise
function quad_elements(nx, ny)
    elts = Vector{Vector{Int}}()
    for j in 1:(ny - 1), i in 1:(nx - 1)
        n1 = (j - 1)*nx + i
        push!(elts, [n1, n1 + 1, n1 + nx + 1, n1 + nx])
    end
    return elts
end
elts = quad_elements(nx, ny)

mesh = build_mesh(nodes, elts)


viz_mesh(mesh, title = "Measurement mesh", zlim = (-0.05, 0.05))










Tip



Any mesh can be used, including meshes coming from a FE software or from an experimental setup, as long as the nodes are numbered from 1 to the number of nodes. Triangles and quadrangles can be mixed. If the numbering is not contiguous, renumber_element_connectivity fixes the connectivity.

title: Visualizing and animating deflection shapes
text:
3 Step 3 – Displaying mode shapes
The mode shapes are evaluated at the nodes of the mesh. To display a deformed mesh, deformed_grid needs a displacement vector with three components per node (\(u_x\), \(u_y\), \(u_z\), node after node): for a plate in bending, only \(u_z\) is non-zero.

Φ = modeshape(plate, kn, xp, yp) # One row per node, one column per mode

# Helper: out-of-plane displacement field → 3 components per node
function out_of_plane!(w)
    u = zeros(3length(w))
    u[3:3:end] .= w
    return u
end

function show_shape(w, title; scale = 0.03)
    w = w/maximum(abs, w)                                # Unit maximum
    deformed = deformed_grid(nodes, out_of_plane!(w), scale)
    return viz_mesh(SimpleMesh(deformed, mesh.topology.connec), color = w, title = title,
                    zlim = (-0.05, 0.05))
end


show_shape(Φ[:, 1], "Mode 1 – (1, 1) – $(round(ωn[1]/2π, digits = 1)) Hz")





show_shape(Φ[:, 4], "Mode 4 – (3, 1) – $(round(ωn[4]/2π, digits = 1)) Hz")




The color map highlights the nodal lines, where the displacement vanishes. They are the places to avoid when choosing excitation or measurement points.

title: Visualizing and animating deflection shapes
text:
4 Step 4 – Operational deflection shapes
A structure excited at a given frequency does not vibrate according to a single mode shape, but according to an operational deflection shape (ODS), which combines the contributions of all the modes. The ODS at frequency \(f\) is given by a column of the FRF matrix: the response of all the nodes to a force applied at one point.

# Point force at (x, y) = (0.15, 0.10) m
i_exc = argmin((xp .- 0.15).^2 .+ (yp .- 0.1).^2)
freq = 1.:0.5:300.
H = solve(ModalFRFProblem(ωn, 0.01, freq, Φ, Φ[i_exc:i_exc, :]), progress = false).u

# ODS at 60 Hz, between modes 2 (43 Hz) and 3 (69 Hz)
i60 = findfirst(>=(60.), freq)
ods_complex = H[:, 1, i60]
ods = real_normalization(reshape(ods_complex, :, 1))[:, 1] # Complex → real shape


show_shape(ods, "ODS at 60 Hz")




The MAC with each mode shape quantifies the contribution of the modes to the ODS.

mac_ods = [mac(ods, Φ[:, k])[1] for k in 1:6]

fig = Figure()
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "Mode", ylabel = "MAC with the ODS at 60 Hz", xticks = 1:6)
barplot!(ax, 1:6, mac_ods)
ylims!(ax, 0., 1.)
fig




The ODS at 60 Hz is dominated by modes 3 and 2, the two modes surrounding the excitation frequency, but neither of them alone describes it. This is why an ODS should never be confused with a mode shape, unless the excitation frequency is very close to an isolated resonance.

title: Visualizing and animating deflection shapes
text:
5 Step 5 – Animating a deflection shape
animate_mesh records a video of the harmonic motion of a deflection shape.
w = ods/maximum(abs, ods)
animate_mesh(nodes, elts, out_of_plane!(w), color = w, scale_factor = 0.03, zlim = (-0.05, 0.05),
             title = "ODS at 60 Hz", framerate = 24, frequency = 4., filename = "plate_ods.mp4")

The same function also animates a time or frequency evolution: if values is a matrix with one column per time step (or frequency), and the corresponding vector is given as fourth argument, the title of the video displays the current time (or frequency).
animate_mesh(nodes, elts, U, t, unit_x = "s", quantity_y = "Time", filename = "response.mp4")






Tip



With GLMakie, the 3D views can be rotated and zoomed interactively, which is very convenient to inspect complex shapes. CairoMakie is better suited to static figures for reports.


Reference pages: Extensions, Operational deflection shapes, Mechanical models.

title: Experimental modal analysis
text:
NoteIn this tutorial




You will learn how to identify the natural frequencies, damping ratios and mode shapes of a structure from measured FRFs, and how to validate the identified modal model.
Prerequisites: the Getting started page. The virtual testing tutorial explains how FRFs are measured.
Duration: about 20 minutes.
Experimental Modal Analysis (EMA) consists in fitting a modal model to measured Frequency Response Functions (FRFs). Because we work here with synthetic data, the exact modal parameters are known, and we can check every step of the identification.

title: Experimental modal analysis
text:
1 Step 1 – The measured FRFs
We consider a simply supported steel beam, equipped with 19 accelerometers regularly spaced every 5 cm and excited by an impact hammer at \(x\) = 0.15 m. The hammer location coincides with the 3rd accelerometer: this driving point will be needed to scale the mode shapes.

# Structure
L, b, h = 1., 0.03, 0.01
beam = Beam(L, b*h, b*h^3/12, 2.1e11, 7850.)
ξ = 0.01

# Test setup
x_acc = collect(0.05:0.05:0.95)   # 19 accelerometers
x_hit = [0.15]                    # Impact location = 3rd accelerometer
dpi = [3, 1]                      # Driving point: (accelerometer 3, impact 1)

# Exact modal basis (ground truth), including modes above the analysis band
fmax = 1000.
ωn, kn = modefreq(beam, 4fmax)
Φ_acc = modeshape(beam, kn, x_acc)
Φ_hit = modeshape(beam, kn, x_hit)

To keep this tutorial short, the noisy accelerances are generated directly in the frequency domain, with a signal-to-noise ratio of 40 dB. The virtual testing tutorial shows how to obtain them from simulated time signals.

freq = 1.:0.5:fmax
H_exact = solve(ModalFRFProblem(ωn, ξ, freq, Φ_acc, Φ_hit), type = :acc, progress = false).u
H = agwn(H_exact, 40.) # Array of size (19 accelerometers × 1 impact × nf)

# Ground truth in the analysis band
in_band = ωn .< 2π*fmax
fn_exact = ωn[in_band]/2π
Φ_exact = Φ_acc[:, in_band]
nmodes = length(fn_exact)


fig = Figure()
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "Frequency (Hz)", ylabel = "Accelerance (dB, ref: 1 m/s²/N)",
          title = "Measured FRFs (19 accelerometers)")
for i in axes(H, 1)
    lines!(ax, freq, to_dB.(H[i, 1, :]), color = (:gray, 0.4))
end
lines!(ax, freq, to_dB.(H[dpi[1], 1, :]), label = "Driving point FRF")
xlims!(ax, 0., fmax)
axislegend(ax, position = :rb)
fig

title: Experimental modal analysis
text:
2 Step 2 – Defining the EMA problem
All the identification methods take an EMAProblem as input. It gathers the FRFs, the frequency vector and, importantly, the type of FRF.

prob = EMAProblem(H, freq, type_frf = :acc)







WarningPitfall



The modal model fitted by the identification methods is formulated for admittances (displacement/force). EMAProblem converts the FRFs internally, but only if you tell it what you provide. Forgetting type_frf = :acc does not raise any error, but biases the results, as shown below for the damping ratio of the first mode.



for (label, p) in [("type_frf = :acc ", EMAProblem(H, freq, type_frf = :acc)),
                   ("type_frf omitted", EMAProblem(H, freq))]
    stable_poles = stabilization(p, 30, LSCF()).poles[end]   # See Step 3
    fn, ξn = poles2modal(stable_poles[.!isnan.(stable_poles)])
    println(label, " → mode 1: f = ", round(fn[1], digits = 2), " Hz, ξ = ", round(100ξn[1], digits = 2),
            " % (exact: ", 100ξ, " %)")
end

type_frf = :acc  → mode 1: f = 23.41 Hz, ξ = 0.96 % (exact: 1.0 %)
type_frf omitted → mode 1: f = 23.48 Hz, ξ = 0.6 % (exact: 1.0 %)

title: Experimental modal analysis
text:
3 Step 3 – Stabilization diagram
The identification methods of the LSCF family require a model order, i.e. the number of modes of the fitted model. This number is unknown in practice, and overestimating it creates spurious, non-physical poles. The stabilization diagram solves this problem: the poles are computed for increasing model orders, and the physical poles are those that remain stable (in frequency and damping) from one order to the next.

stab = stabilization(prob, 30, LSCF())
stabilization_plot(stab)




The vertical alignments of stable poles indicate the physical modes. The background curve is the PSIF (Power Spectrum Indicator Function), which summarizes all the FRFs and helps to locate the resonances. Six physical modes clearly appear in the frequency band.
The poles that are stable at the highest model order are retained.

poles = stab.poles[end]
poles = poles[.!isnan.(poles)]    # Unstable poles are flagged as NaN
fn_id, ξn_id = poles2modal(poles)


data = hcat(string.(eachindex(fn_id)), round.(fn_exact[eachindex(fn_id)], digits = 2),
            round.(fn_id, digits = 2), round.(100ξn_id, digits = 2))

pretty_table(
    HTML,
    data,
    column_labels = ["Mode", "f exact (Hz)", "f identified (Hz)", "ξ identified (%)"],
    alignment = :c
)

title: Experimental modal analysis
text:
4 Step 4 – Mode shapes
Once the poles are known, the mode shapes are obtained by fitting each resonance peak of the FRFs. Here, we use a single-degree-of-freedom least-squares fit (LSFit) in the vicinity of each identified natural frequency. Thanks to the driving point, the mode shapes are mass-normalized, and can therefore be directly compared with the exact ones.

Φ_id = modeshape_extraction(prob, poles, LSFit(), dpi = dpi)


fig = Figure(size = (700, 600))
for i in 1:nmodes
    axi = Axis(fig[(i - 1) ÷ 2 + 1, (i - 1) % 2 + 1], title = "Mode $i – $(round(fn_id[i], digits = 1)) Hz")
    lines!(axi, x_acc, Φ_exact[:, i], label = "Exact")
    scatter!(axi, x_acc, Φ_id[:, i], color = :orange, label = "Identified")
    xlims!(axi, 0., L)
    i == 1 && axislegend(axi, position = :cb)
end
fig

title: Experimental modal analysis
text:
5 Step 5 – Validation with the MAC
The Modal Assurance Criterion (MAC) measures the correlation between two mode shapes: 1 means that the shapes are identical (up to a scaling factor), 0 that they are orthogonal. In practice, a MAC above 0.9 is considered a good match.

MAC = mac(Φ_id, Φ_exact)

fig = Figure()
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "Identified mode", ylabel = "Exact mode", title = "MAC matrix",
          xticks = 1:nmodes, yticks = 1:nmodes, aspect = DataAspect())
hm = heatmap!(ax, 1:nmodes, 1:nmodes, MAC, colorrange = (0, 1), colormap = :Blues)
for i in 1:nmodes, j in 1:nmodes
    text!(ax, i, j, text = string(round(MAC[i, j], digits = 2)), align = (:center, :center),
          color = MAC[i, j] > 0.5 ? :white : :black, fontsize = 12)
end
Colorbar(fig[1, 2], hm)
fig




A diagonal MAC matrix with values close to 1 indicates that each identified mode matches one exact mode, and only one.






Tip



Without a reference model, the MAC is computed between the identified mode shapes themselves (mac(Φ_id, Φ_id), the AutoMAC). Large off-diagonal terms then reveal either a spatial aliasing (too few measurement points) or a spurious mode.

title: Experimental modal analysis
text:
6 Step 6 – FRF synthesis
The final check consists in rebuilding the FRFs from the identified modal model and comparing them with the measured ones. The residues of the modal model are computed from the mass-normalized mode shapes.

res = mode2residues(Φ_id, poles, 1:length(x_acc), [dpi[1]])[1]
H_synth = frf_reconstruction(res, poles, freq, type = :acc)


fig = Figure()
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1], xlabel = "Frequency (Hz)", ylabel = "Accelerance (dB, ref: 1 m/s²/N)",
          title = "Accelerometer at x = $(x_acc[7]) m")
lines!(ax, freq, to_dB.(H[7, 1, :]), label = "Measured")
lines!(ax, freq, to_dB.(H_synth[7, 1, :]), linestyle = :dash, label = "Synthesized")
xlims!(ax, 0., fmax)
axislegend(ax, position = :rb)
fig




The synthesized FRF follows the measurement over the whole band. The small differences near the anti-resonances come from the modes located outside the analysis band, which are not included in the modal model.

title: Experimental modal analysis
section: 7 Step 7 – Why the type of FRF matters
text:
7 Step 7 – Why the type of FRF matters
In the Getting started page, we used accelerances rather than admittances. Let us see why, by adding the same 40 dB noise to the admittances.

H_dis = agwn(solve(ModalFRFProblem(ωn, ξ, freq, Φ_acc, Φ_hit), progress = false).u, 40.)
stab_dis = stabilization(EMAProblem(H_dis, freq), 30, LSCF())
poles_dis = stab_dis.poles[end]
poles_dis = poles_dis[.!isnan.(poles_dis)]

println("Modes identified from accelerances: ", round.(fn_id, digits = 1))
println("Modes identified from admittances:  ", round.(poles2modal(poles_dis)[1], digits = 1))

Modes identified from accelerances: [23.4, 93.8, 211.1, 375.3, 586.4, 844.3]
Modes identified from admittances:  [23.5, 93.8, 211.1, 375.2, 586.0]


The admittance of a beam decreases roughly as \(1/\omega^2\) above the first resonance. For a given SNR defined over the whole band, the high-frequency modes of the admittance are therefore buried in the noise, and the last mode is lost. Accelerances, whose level is much more uniform over the frequency band, do not suffer from this problem. This is also why accelerometers are the sensors of choice for modal testing.

title: Experimental modal analysis
text:
8 Summary
A complete EMA follows these steps:

Define an EMAProblem with the right type_frf.
Build a stabilization diagram (stabilization + stabilization_plot) and select the stable poles.
Extract the mode shapes (modeshape_extraction), using a driving point to scale them.
Validate with the MAC (mac) and with an FRF synthesis (mode2residues + frf_reconstruction).

Next step: when the excitation cannot be measured, the same modal parameters can be identified from the responses only. See Operational modal analysis.
Reference pages: Modal extraction, Modal indicators.

title: Installation
text:
Note



If you are already a Julia user, you can skip this section.
This section explains how to install Julia and StructuralVibration.jl.

title: Installation
text:
Install Julia 
There exists several ways of installing Julia and managing versions. The recommended way consists in installing juliaup, which is a Julia version manager.

Windows
On Windows, juliaup can be installed directly from the Windows store or from a terminal by typing the following command:
winget install julia -s msstore
MacOS and Linux
On MacOS and Linux, juliaup can be installed from a terminal by typing:
curl -fsSL https://install.julialang.org | sh
or by using software repositories:
# MacOS
brew install juliaup

# Arch-based distributions
yay -S juliaup

Once juliaup is installed, the latest version of Julia can be installed from a terminal as follows:
juliaup add release

title: Installation
text:
Install StructuralVibration.jl 
The package is registered in the Julia General Registry. So, to install the package, you can use the following command:
(Yourenv) pkg> add StructuralVibration

title: Digital Signal Processing
text: StructuralVibration.jl provides a set of functions complementing the DSP.jl to simulate the signal processing pipelines used in structural dynamics applications, such as modal analysis, system identification, and vibration data processing. They can for instance be used to simulate or to process experimental data, which can then be used to validate new algorithms (direct or inverse methods) and to benchmark with existing ones.

title: Digital Signal Processing
text:
1 Window functions
The DSP.jl package provides a set of window functions that can be used to reduce spectral leakage in the frequency domain. The StructuralVibration.jl package exports the window functions defined in DSP.jl and provides additional ones for the sake of completeness.

1.1 Windows from DSP.jl

1.1.1 Rectangular window
The rectangular window is the simplest window function, which does not modify the signal. It is defined as: \[
w[n] = 1,
\] for \(n \in [0, N-1]\), where \(N\) is the length of the window.
The rectangular window is generally not recommended for spectral analysis, as it introduces significant spectral leakage. It is mainly used for testing purposes or when no windowing is required (such as impact testing for sufficiently long acquisition duration).

1.1.1.1 API

rect



rect
Rectangular window
Exported from DSP.jl








1.1.1.2 Example

rectwin = rect(1024)









1.1.2 Hann(ing) window
The Hann window is a raised cosine window that tapers the signal at both ends. It is defined as: \[
w[n] = \frac{1}{2} \left[1 - \cos\left(\frac{2\pi n}{N-1}\right)\right],
\] where \(N\) is the length of the window and \(n \in [0, N-1]\).

1.1.2.1 API

hann



hann
Hann(ing) window
Exported from DSP.jl








1.1.2.2 Example

hannwin = hanning(1024)









1.1.3 Hamming window
The Hamming window is a raised cosine window that tapers the signal at both ends. It is defined as: \[
w[n] = 0.54 - 0.46 \cos\left(\frac{2\pi n}{N-1}\right),
\] where \(N\) is the length of the window and \(n \in [0, N-1]\).

1.1.3.1 API

hamming



hamming
Hamming window
Exported from DSP.jl








1.1.3.2 Example

hammwin = hamming(1024)









1.1.4 Tukey window
The Tukey window (also known as the cosine-tapered window) is defined by a tapering parameter \(\alpha \in [0,1]\), which controls the proportion of the window that is tapered. The window is defined as:
\[
\begin{align*}
& w[n] = \frac{1}{2} \left[1 - \cos\left(\frac{2\pi n}{\alpha(N-1)}\right)\right], & 0 \leq n < \frac{\alpha(N-1)}{2} \\
& w[n] = 1,  & \frac{\alpha(N-1)}{2} \leq n \leq \frac{(N-1)}{2} \\
& w[N-1 - n] = w[n], & 0 \leq n \leq \frac{\alpha(N-1)}{2} \\
\end{align*}
\]
When \(\alpha = 0\), the Tukey window becomes a rectangular window, and when \(\alpha = 1\), it becomes equivalent to a Hann window.

1.1.4.1 API

tukey



tukey
Tukey window
Exported from DSP.jl








1.1.4.2 Example

tukeywin = tukey(1024, 0.5)









1.1.5 Cosine window
The cosine window is a raised cosine window that tapers the signal at both ends. It is defined as: \[
w[n] = \cos\left(\frac{\pi n}{N-1} - \frac{\pi}{2}\right),
\] where \(N\) is the length of the window and \(n \in [0, N-1]\).

1.1.5.1 API

cosine



cosine
Cosine window
Exported from DSP.jl








1.1.5.2 Example

coswin = cosine(1024)









1.1.6 Lanczos window
The Lanczos window is a raised cosine window that tapers the signal at both ends. It is defined as: \[
w[n] = \text{sinc}\left(\frac{2n}{N-1} - 1\right),
\] where \(N\) is the length of the window and \(n \in [0, N-1]\).

1.1.6.1 API

lanczos



lanczos
Lanczos window
Exported from DSP.jl








1.1.6.2 Example

lanczoswin = lanczos(1024)









1.1.7 Triangular window
The triangular window is a simple window function that tapers the signal at both ends. It is defined as: \[
w[n] = 1 - \frac{|2n - (N-1)|}{L},
\] where \(L = N/N+1\) if \(N\) is even/odd and \(n \in [0, N-1]\).

1.1.7.1 API

triang



triang
Triangle window
Exported from DSP.jl







triangwin = triang(1024)









1.1.8 Bartlett window
The Bartlett window is a triangular window that tapers the signal at both ends. It is defined as: \[
w[n] = \left(1 - \frac{|n - L|}{L}\right),
\] where \(L = \frac{N-1}{2}\) and \(n \in [0, N-1]\).

1.1.8.1 API

bartlett



bartlett
Bartlett window
Exported from DSP.jl








1.1.8.2 Example

bartlettwin = bartlett(1024)









1.1.9 Bartlett-Hann window
The Bartlett-Hann window is a raised cosine window that tapers the signal at both ends. It is defined as: \[
w[n] = 0.62 - 0.48 \left|\frac{n}{N-1} - 0.5\right| + 0.38 \cos\left(2\pi\left[\frac{n}{N-1} - 0.5\right]\right),
\] where \(n \in [0, N-1]\).

1.1.9.1 API

bartlett_hann



bartlett_hann
Bartlett-Hann window
Exported from DSP.jl








1.1.9.2 Example

barthannwin = bartlett_hann(1024)









1.1.10 Gaussian window
The Gaussian window is a raised cosine window that tapers the signal at both ends. It is defined as: \[
w[n] = \text{exp}\left(-\frac{(n - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right),
\] where \(\mu = \frac{N-1}{2}\) is the center of the window, \(\sigma\) is the standard deviation, and \(n \in [0, N-1]\).

1.1.10.1 API

gaussian



gaussian
Gaussian window
Exported from DSP.jl








1.1.10.2 Example

gaussianwin = gaussian(1024, 0.2)









1.1.11 Blackman window
The Blackman window is a raised cosine window that tapers the signal at both ends. It is defined as: \[
w[n] = 0.42 - 0.5 \cos\left(\frac{2\pi n}{N-1}\right) + 0.08 \cos\left(\frac{4\pi n}{N-1}\right),
\] where \(n \in [0, N-1]\).

1.1.11.1 API

blackman



blackman
Blackman window
Exported from DSP.jl








1.1.11.2 Example

blackmanwin = blackman(1024)









1.1.12 Kaiser window
The Kaiser window is a raised cosine window that tapers the signal at both ends. It is defined as: \[
w[n] = I_0\left(\pi\alpha \sqrt{1 - \left(\frac{2n}{N-1} - 1\right)^2}\right) / I_0(\pi\alpha),
\] where \(I_0\) is the modified Bessel function of the first kind, \(\beta\) is a parameter that controls the shape of the window, and \(n \in [0, N-1]\).

1.1.12.1 API

kaiser



kaiser
Kaiser window
Exported from DSP.jl








1.1.12.2 Example

kaiserwin = kaiser(1024, 0.5)









1.1.13 DPSS window
The DPSS (Discrete Prolate Spheroidal Sequences) window maximizes the energy concentration in the main lobe. It has no closed form expression and depends on two parameters: the length of the window \(N\) and the time-half-bandwidth product \(Nw\) which controls the energy concentration in the main lobe.

1.1.13.1 API

dpss



dpss
DPSS window
Exported from DSP.jl








1.1.13.2 Example

dpsswin = dpss(1024, 4, 1)










1.2 Additional window functions

1.2.1 Exponential window
An exponential window is a window function that tapers the signal exponentially. It is defined as: \[
w[n] = \text{exp}\left(-\frac{\tau n}{N-1}\right),
\] where \(n \in [0, N-1]\), \(\tau = -\log(p)\) is the time constant, and \(p\) is the percentage of the original value by the end of the acquisition block.

1.2.1.1 API

exponential



exponential(N, exponential_end = 0.01)
Create an exponential window. exponential_end = 1 is a uniform window.
Inputs

N: Number of points

exponential_end: End value of the exponential window (0 < exponential_end <= 1)


Output

w: Exponential window










1.2.1.2 Example

exponentialwin = exponential(1024, 0.1)









1.2.2 Force window
The force window is a window function particularly useful in impact testing, where the input signal is a short impulse. The force window is the product of two distinct windows. The first one, denoted \(w_1[n]\), is a rectangular window whose end is tapered by a cosine function, namely: \[
w_1[n] = \begin{cases}
1, & 0 \leq n < L \\
\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\left(\frac{n - L}{M - L}\right)\right), & L \leq n < M \\
0, & M \leq n < N
\end{cases},
\] where \(n \in [0, N-1]\), \(L = pN\) is the width of the window, \(M = N\text{min}(1, L/N + 0.04)\) is the index of the end of the cosine tapering part of the window, and \(p\) is the percentage of the length of the data acquisition block.
The second one, denoted \(w_2[n]\), is the exponentital window defined above. Hence, the force window is defined as: \[
w[n] = w_1[n] \cdot w_2[n],
\] where \(w_2[n] = \text{exp}\left(-\frac{\tau n}{N-1}\right)\), with \(\tau = -\log(p)\).

1.2.2.1 API

force



force(N, width = 0.1, exponential_end = 0.01)
Create a force window according to Ref.[1].  For modal testing the exponential_end should be the same in the force and in the exponential window.
Inputs

N: Number of points

width: Width (fraction) of the force window (between 0 and 1)

exponential_end: End value of the exponential window (0 < exponential_end <= 1)


Output

w: Force window


Note
exponential_end = 1 does not apply any exponential decay.
Reference
[1] W. A. Fladung and R. W. Rost. Cause and effect of applying the exponential window to an impact force signal. In Proceedings of IMAC XIV. Orlando, United States. 1996.








1.2.2.2 Example

forcewin = force(1024, 0.2, 1.)
force_expwin = force(1024, 0.2, 0.01)









1.2.3 Flat-top window
The flat-top window is a window function that window is a partially negative-valued window that has minimal scalloping loss in the frequency domain. It is defined as: \[
w[n] = a_0 - a_1\cos\left(\frac{2\pi n}{N-1}\right) + a_2\cos\left(\frac{4\pi n}{N-1}\right) - a_3\cos\left(\frac{6\pi n}{N-1}\right) + a_4\cos\left(\frac{8\pi n}{N-1}\right),
\] where \(n \in [0, N-1]\) and \(a_0 = 0.21557895\), \(a_1 = 0.41663158\), \(a_2 = 0.277263158\), \(a_3 = 0.083578947\), and \(a_4 = 0.006947368\).

1.2.3.1 API

flattop



flattop(N)
Create a flat top window
Input

N: Number of points


Output

w: Flattop window










1.2.3.2 Example

flattopwin = flattop(1024)









1.2.4 Nuttall window
The Nutall window is a window function that returns a Nuttall four-term symmetric Blackman-Harris window. It produces slightly lower sidelobes than Blackman-Harris window. It is defined as: \[
w[n] = a_0 - a_1\cos\left(\frac{2\pi n}{N-1}\right) + a_2\cos\left(\frac{4\pi n}{N-1}\right) - a_3\cos\left(\frac{6\pi n}{N-1}\right),
\] where \(n \in [0, N-1]\) and \(a_0 = 0.355768\), \(a_1 = 0.487396\), \(a_2 = 0.144232\), and \(a_3 = 0.012604\).

1.2.4.1 API

nuttall



nuttall(N)
Create a Nuttall window
Input

N: Number of points


Output

w: Nuttall window










1.2.4.2 Example

nuttallwin = nuttall(1024)









1.2.5 Blackman-Nuttall window
The Blackman-Nuttall window is a window function that is a modified version of the exact Blackman window. It is defined as: \[
w[n] = a_0 - a_1\cos\left(\frac{2\pi n}{N-1}\right) + a_2\cos\left(\frac{4\pi n}{N-1}\right) - a_3\cos\left(\frac{6\pi n}{N-1}\right),
\] where \(n \in [0, N-1]\) and \(a_0 = 0.3635819\), \(a_1 = 0.4891775\), \(a_2 = 0.1365995\), and \(a_3 = 0.0106411\).

1.2.5.1 API

blackman_nuttall



blackman_nuttall(N)
Create a Blackman-Nuttall window
Input

N: Number of points


Output

w: Blackman-Nutall window










1.2.5.2 Example

blackman_nuttallwin = blackman_nuttall(1024)









1.2.6 Blackman-Harris window
The Blackman-Harris window is a window function that is another modified version of the exact Blackman window. It is defined as: \[
w[n] = a_0 - a_1\cos\left(\frac{2\pi n}{N-1}\right) + a_2\cos\left(\frac{4\pi n}{N-1}\right) - a_3\cos\left(\frac{6\pi n}{N-1}\right),
\] where \(n \in [0, N-1]\) and \(a_0 = 0.35875\), \(a_1 = 0.48829\), \(a_2 = 0.14128\), and \(a_3 = 0.01168\).

1.2.6.1 API

blackman_harris



blackman_harris(N)
Create a Blackman-Harris window
Input

N: Number of points


Output

w: Blackman-Harris window










1.2.6.2 Example

blackman_harriswin = blackman_harris(1024)









1.2.7 Parzen window
The parzen window is a window function is defined as: \[
w[n] = \begin{cases}
1 - 6\left(\frac{2|n - M|}{N}\right)^2\left(1 - \frac{2|n - M|}{N}\right) &  0 \leq |n - M| \leq \frac{M}{2}\\
2\left(1 - \frac{2|n - M|}{N}\right)^3 & \frac{M}{2} < |n - M| \leq M\\
\end{cases}
\] where \(M = \frac{N - 1}{2}\) and \(n \in [0, N-1]\).

1.2.7.1 API

parzen



parzen(N)
Create a Parzen window
Input

N: Number of points


Output

w: Parzen window










1.2.7.2 Example

parzenwin = parzen(1024)









1.2.8 Planck-taper window
The Planck-taper window is a window function that is defined as: \[
w[n] = \begin{cases}
0, & n = 0 \\
(1 + \text{exp}\left(\frac{\epsilon N}{n} - \frac{\epsilon N}{\epsilon N - n}\right)), & 1 \leq n < \epsilon N \\
1, & \epsilon N \leq n < N/2 \\
w[N - n], & 0 \leq n < N/2 \\
\end{cases},
\] where \(n \in [0, N-1]\) and \(\epsilon\) is a parameter, defined in [0, 1] that controls the amount of tapering

1.2.8.1 API

planck



planck(N, ϵ = 0.25)
Create a Planck-taper window
Inputs

N: Number of points

ϵ: Parameter controlling the tapering


Output

w: Planck-taper window










1.2.8.2 Example

planckwin = planck(1024, 0.1)









1.2.9 Flat triangular window
The flat triangular window is a window function that is defined as: \[
w[n] = \begin{cases}
1 & 0 \leq n < L \\
\frac{N - n}{N - L} & L \leq n \leq N \\
\end{cases},
\] where \(n \in [0, N-1]\) and \(L = pN\) is the width of the flat part of the window, with \(p\) being the percentage of the length of the data acquisition block.

planck



flattri(N, width = 0.5)
Create a flat triangular window
Inputs

N: Number of points

width: Width (fraction) of the flat part of the window (between 0 and 1)


Output

w: Flat triangle window










1.2.9.2 Example

flattriwin = flattri(1024, 0.25)










1.3 Choice of a window function
The choice of a window function depends on the application and the desired properties of the window1 2 3. Here are some general guidelines for the main windows used in structural dynamics applications:

Rectangular window: This window is suitable for signals which are periodic in the acquisition window or for non-periodic signals which tend to 0 whithin the time window (such as impact testing).
Hann window: This window is suitable for noisy signals. It is generally used with random signal due to its moderate impact on the frequency resolution and amplitude accuracy of porcessed signals.
Hamming window: This window is used in case of noisy measured signals as the Hann windows. However, contrary to the Hann window, the Hamming window doesn’t reach zero at its both ends.
Tukey window: This window is generally used to analyze transient data due to its shape, since it limits the alteration of the amplitude of transient signals.
Blackman-Harris window: This window is suitable for periodic measurement signals.
Flat-top window: This window is suitable for a calibration purposes (good reproduction of the amplitude height) and for measurements with sine excitation. However, it is not suitable for very noisy measurement signals.
Force window: This window is an effective mechanism for reducing noise on the input channel when the input signal is impulsive.
Exponential window: This window is suitable for transient signals that decay to zero, such as acceleration signal in impact testing.

title: Digital Signal Processing
